title: Purdue’s IDEAS Lab Builds Autonomous Drone That Tracks People Through Forests Without GPS
summary:
Purdue University engineers have demonstrated a new unmanned aircraft capable of following targets in densely wooded areas without relying on external signals. The drone pursues human targets independently, utilizing onboard computing to generate 3D maps of the terrain and predict a target's direction when visual contact is lost, all while flying roughly 2 meters above the ground at jogging speed.

The hardware was developed by Purdue’s IDEAS Lab, which integrated open-source software from the University of Hong Kong to enable the system's autonomous navigation. The project aligns with a $1.5 million contract between the lab and the U.S. Army to build autonomous ground and aerial robots for scouting threats in hostile environments where communications and GPS are jammed or unavailable.

selectedTweets.text:
WATCH: A drone chases a running person through a dense forest with no GPS, no internet, and no human steering it. 

The drone flies about 2 meters off the ground at jogging speed, builds a 3D map of the trees as it goes, and guesses where the person is headed when trees block its view. 

Everything runs on board the drone itself. 

Purdue’s IDEAS Lab built the hardware, but the software leans on open-source tools, mostly from the University of Hong Kong, so it isn’t entirely made from scratch. 

The same lab also has a separate $1.5 million Army research deal for robots that work without GPS. https://t.co/ElLqOjX3KD
